name: stoic-analogy
motion: A hospital should be allowed to let an AI triage system decide which patients are seen first, even where no clinician can explain a given ordering.
argument: A ship's captain in a storm does not get to choose the weather. He chooses the set of the sail, and he is judged on that choice and on nothing else. Hand him a chart he cannot read and he is still judged on the set of the sail, because that is still what is his. The triage system is the weather. Whether it orders the queue well is not up to the clinician standing beside it; what is up to her is whether she consented to stand there, whether she said plainly that she cannot account for the ordering, and whether she keeps looking. Her consent comes first of those, and it has to be just: justice is owed to the patients, not to her wish to explain everything she touches. She consents because they are owed a clinician at the point where the queue is decided, one who tells them the truth and keeps watch, and refusing the post so as never to answer for an ordering she cannot explain would leave them with the system and no one beside it. A clinician who uses the system and tells the truth about it has done the part that was hers. A clinician who hides behind it has not, and no accuracy figure repairs that, because the figure was never the thing she was answerable for.
